questions.q: Define 'informal economy' as described in the NCERT textbook and give one example of a worker in this sector.
questions.a: The informal economy refers to transactions outside the sphere of regular employment, sometimes involving cash for services but often direct exchange of goods/services, unrecorded in official employment statistics. Example: a street vendor selling vegetables without a licence or a home-based beedi roller paid per piece. A wrong answer (e.g., 'unorganised sector is just small factories') reveals confusion between 'informal' (legal/regulatory status) and 'unorganised' (enterprise size), a common conflation in Indian policy discourse.

questions.q: Explain why the textbook says 'the vast majority of people in modern societies do not produce the food they eat, the houses they live in, or the material goods they consume' and how this relates to division of labour.
questions.a: Modern societies exhibit an enormous expansion of economic interdependence: each person specialises in one narrow occupation and relies on countless other specialised workers worldwide for their needs. This is the essence of a highly complex division of labour. A wrong answer focusing only on 'technology' or 'trade' misses the sociological point that division of labour is a social arrangement structuring dependence and power, not merely a technical efficiency.

questions.q: A garment factory in Tamil Nadu supplies a European brand. The brand demands a 5% price cut; the factory owner says wages cannot be cut further without violating minimum wage law. Using the Bangalore garment industry case, explain why the factory owner may still resist union demands for higher wages even if the brand agrees to pay more.
questions.a: The factory is one link in a long supply chain where the manufacturer controls only 15 of 100+ operations. If wages rise, the brand can shift orders to another locality or country with lower costs, making the factory uncompetitive. Thus the owner's freedom is 'extremely limited' by global buyer power. A wrong answer blaming only 'greedy owners' ignores the structural constraint of global competition that the textbook explicitly highlights.

questions.q: Compare the division of labour in a traditional craft (e.g., handloom weaving) with that in a modern assembly line. Identify two consequences for the worker's skill, autonomy, and relationship to the final product.
questions.a: Craft: worker controls entire process, uses holistic skill, decides pace, identifies with final product. Assembly line: worker performs one simplified, timed operation, no control over pace, alienated from final product. Consequences: (1) deskilling – craft knowledge replaced by repetitive motion; (2) loss of autonomy – surveillance and timing replace self-regulation. A wrong answer that says 'assembly line is just faster' misses the qualitative transformation of the labour process and worker experience.

questions.q: Evaluate the functionalist claim that 'modern industrial societies function best if women look after the family and men earn the family livelihood' using evidence from the textbook about women in the garment export industry.
questions.a: The functionalist claim is empirically false: the textbook states 'in contemporary industries like the garment export, women form a large part of the labour force', contradicting the presumed gendered separation. Moreover, female-headed households (due to migration, widowhood, or desertion) show women as sole providers. The claim also ignores that the 'male breadwinner' model was historically specific to certain Western industrial societies, not universal. A wrong answer merely saying 'it's sexist' fails to use the textbook's empirical counter-evidence.

questions.q: Design a mini-research plan to study how the separation of work and home affects the daily time-use of women in an informal settlement. Specify: (a) one quantitative method, (b) one qualitative method, and (c) how you would link findings to the textbook's concept of 'unintended consequences' of economic change.
questions.a: (a) Time-use survey with 24-hour recall for 50 women, categorising paid work, unpaid care, commute, leisure. (b) In-depth interviews with 10 women about strategies for managing work/home overlap and perceived changes over a generation. (c) Link to 'unintended consequences' by showing how factory shifts (economic change) lengthen commutes, reduce childcare time, and force reliance on older siblings or informal crèches – outcomes not planned by factory owners or state policy. A poor answer would list methods without connecting to the sociological concept.
